traveler: Ann Lee (Ann Lees, called Mother Ann)
title: The Mill and the Wilderness: Mother Ann from Toad Lane to Niskayuna
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Manchester, birth on the leap day
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia, Appletons' Cyclopaedia and the National Park Service all give 29 February 1736; the Toad Lane address is Shaker tradition and is documented nowhere
stops.campa: A blacksmith's daughter is born in Manchester on the leap day, the second of eight children, in a house that keeps no record of itself. Shaker tradition sets the birth on Toad Lane. She is never taught to read or write, and will sign her name with a mark. Around the cradle the first industrial city on earth is assembling itself out of cotton, coal, and water, and the children of the town go into it at seven and eight years old. A hundred and nine years later Karl Marx will sit at the alcove desk in Chetham's Library, a few streets from this spot, reading the returns of the same mills.
suggested_refs: Toad Lane, Manchester, the traditional birthplace, with no marker or plaque documented in any source
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Manchester Collegiate Church, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested, from the parish register as cited in Wikipedia
stops.campa: At six years old she is carried up to the Collegiate Church at the top of the town and baptized Ann Lees. The register entry is one of only two contemporaneous documents of her whole life. The mill, the fur, the infirmary kitchen, the four small graves, the prison cells: none of it leaves a page written at the time by anybody. She will come back to this church once, at twenty four, to be married in it. The building is now Manchester Cathedral and stands where it stood, above the Irwell, at the oldest corner of the city.
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of the Collegiate Church of Manchester, 1 June 1742

stops.name: Manchester, the cotton mill
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources agree she worked in a Manchester cotton mill as a child but name no mill and no year, and the coordinate is the atlas's canonical Manchester pin, not an address
stops.campa: As a girl she is put into a Manchester cotton mill. No source names the mill, the master, or the year she enters it. The work is twelve hours in lint and noise, and the body learns a rhythm long before the mind is offered letters. Nearly two centuries later Rudolf Laban will come to these same mills to watch factory hands move and to write their effort down in notation. The worship this child grows up to invent is danced, stamped, turned, and shaken until the floorboards give: a body drilled in a mill and then handed back to God.
suggested_refs: The unnamed Manchester cotton mill of her childhood, an honest gap in every account

stops.name: Manchester, cutting fur for the hatters
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the trade is attested, the workshop and the year are not
stops.campa: She goes from the mill to the hatters, cutting fur for the felting trade, where the pelts are carroted with mercury and the old men of the shop shake at their benches. Manchester at midcentury runs on this: children's hands, animal skin, and chemicals nobody has yet named as poison. Hermann Keyserling, travelling in Bengal, will one day write of Calcutta holding Kali and Manchester in one hand. She is nineteen, unlettered, and has now worked two of the trades the city was built on.
suggested_refs: The mercury carroting process of the eighteenth-century hatting trade, and the shaking it produced in its workers

stops.name: Manchester Infirmary at Piccadilly, the kitchen
stops.date_confidence: attested that she cooked at the infirmary around age twenty; the year is approximate and the building is the Lever's Row site at Piccadilly, opened 1755, not the Market Street site named in some summaries
stops.campa: Around twenty she takes a place as a cook at the Manchester Infirmary on Lever's Row at Piccadilly, opened the year before she comes to it. The same building holds the town's lunatic asylum, so the kitchen she works in feeds the sick and the mad off one range. Appletons' Cyclopaedia will report, a century later and alone among the sources, that she was herself shut in a mad-house for what she preached. In 1912 Niels Bohr will arrive in this city to work in Rutherford's laboratory on the interior of the atom.
suggested_refs: The Manchester Infirmary of 1755 at Lever's Row, Piccadilly, which housed the public lunatic asylum in the same fabric
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Manchester, joining the Wardley society
stops.date_confidence: disputed: Wikipedia and the National Park Service give 1758, Appletons' Cyclopaedia gives 1747, when she would have been eleven; the meeting address is recorded nowhere and the coordinate is the canonical Manchester pin
stops.campa: Jane and James Wardley, a tailor and his wife, keep a small society in Manchester whose worship descends from the French prophets of the Cevennes: silence, then shaking, trembling, shouting, and dancing until the meeting is spent. Ann Lees joins them, twenty two years old and unlettered. The neighbours call them the Shaking Quakers, and the name sticks for two hundred and fifty years. Manchester keeps this habit of handing on strange authority in small rooms; in 1902 John Yarker will sign Masonic letters-patent over to Theodor Reuss in this same city.
stops.quote: I love the day when I first received the gospel; I call it my birthday.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. VII
suggested_refs: The Wardley society of Manchester, the Camisard inheritance in English dissent
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Manchester Collegiate Church, the marriage to Abraham Stanley
stops.date_confidence: attested from the parish register as cited in Wikipedia; Encyclopedia.com gives 1762 instead, and Appletons' gives no date at all
stops.campa: At twenty four she marries Abraham Stanley, a blacksmith like her father, in the church where she was baptized. Both are of the parish, both are poor, and the couple move in with the Lees rather than take a house of their own. She signs the register with her mark. This entry is the second and last contemporaneous document of her life. Nothing in it suggests that within ten years the marriage will become the thing she preaches against, and the first possession she asks every convert to give up.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of the Collegiate Church of Manchester, 5 January 1761, signed by Ann Lees with a mark

stops.name: Manchester, the four children
stops.date_confidence: the four births and the four deaths are attested; not one birth or death date survives in any source, and the year given here is a placeholder for a decade
stops.campa: Four children are born to Ann Lee and Abraham Stanley in Manchester. All four die, in infancy or early childhood, and not one date of birth or death survives anywhere in the record. What survives is the account of what the losses did to her: nights of crying out, sweats that soaked the bedding through, and the fixed conviction that the act which made the children was the act that damned her. The Shakers will build the entire doctrine on this bedroom. Whether she drew that conclusion herself, or her followers drew it for her afterwards, no document says.
stops.quote: I cried to God three days and nights without intermission, that He would give me true desires.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. VII
suggested_refs: The four unrecorded graves of the Lees-Stanley children, undated in every source
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Manchester, taken up by the magistrates
stops.date_confidence: the repeated imprisonments are attested; the building is unnamed in every source consulted and the dates of the individual jailings are not recorded
stops.campa: She is taken up repeatedly by the Manchester magistrates: for breaking the Sabbath by dancing and shouting, for disturbing the congregation at the old church, for blasphemy. The building that holds her is not named in any account. The society is small, poor, loud, and led increasingly by a woman, which is enough for a warrant in this decade. Each jailing enlarges her standing among the Shaking Quakers, and Jane and James Wardley, who brought her into the society, begin to defer to her.
suggested_refs: The Manchester House of Correction, proposed but unconfirmed as the site of her jailings

stops.name: Manchester, fourteen days and the revelation
stops.date_confidence: the fourteen-day imprisonment and the revelation are attested by Wikipedia and corroborated by the National Park Service; the month and the building are not recorded
stops.campa: Fourteen days shut up alone, and this is the imprisonment that matters. She comes out with the doctrine finished and never alters a line of it afterwards: that the sexual relation is the root of the fall, that sin must be confessed one by one to a living witness, and that celibacy is not a discipline laid on the faithful but salvation itself. The Shakers date the founding of their church to this cell rather than to a meeting house or a year of incorporation. She is thirty four and has been in the society twelve years.
stops.quote: You must forsake the marriage of the flesh, or you cannot be married to the Lamb, nor have any share in the resurrection of Christ.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. III
suggested_refs: The unidentified Manchester prison of 1770, which Shaker chronology treats as the founding site of the church

stops.name: Manchester, acknowledged Mother in spiritual things
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources place the acknowledgement around 1770 and give no month
stops.campa: Her followers begin to call her Mother in spiritual things, and then simply Mother Ann. Jane and James Wardley step back; the society is hers. She is thirty four years old, cannot read, has buried four children, and is telling a room of Manchester poor that the second appearing of Christ has already occurred, in a woman, in this town. In London a boy of thirteen named William Blake is apprenticed to an engraver and has begun seeing the things he will spend fifty years putting on copper.
stops.quote: I denied myself of every gratification of a carnal nature.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. VII, v. 11
suggested_refs: The title Mother in spiritual things, the earliest formulation of Shaker authority
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Manchester, the vision of America
stops.date_confidence: attested by the National Park Service, which states the 1772 vision flatly; the Manchester location is the canonical city pin and no source narrows it further
stops.campa: A place has been prepared for her and her people in America: that is the whole of the vision and the whole of the plan. She has no money, no correspondent across the water, and no notion of where in that country the place lies. John Hocknell, the only follower with property, sells what he has to pay for the passage of the rest. Between the vision and the sailing lie two more years of Manchester, its magistrates, its mills, and the last of the graves she will dig in England.
suggested_refs: John Hocknell's sale of his property to fund the 1774 emigration

stops.name: Liverpool, the nine go aboard the Mariah
stops.date_confidence: the ship Mariah and the party of nine are attested; no source names the port of departure, and Liverpool is inference from the transatlantic trade of the period
stops.campa: Nine people go aboard the ship Mariah: Ann Lee, her husband Abraham Stanley, her brother William, her niece Nancy, James Whittaker, John Hocknell, Richard Hocknell, James Shepherd, and Mary Partington. The ship's name and the passenger list come down; the port does not, and Liverpool is the guess of everyone who has looked since. The captain threatens to put them ashore for dancing on his deck. They are leaving a country in which the whole visible church numbers a few dozen people and owns nothing.
suggested_refs: The ship Mariah, named in the sources but with no surviving manifest or port of clearance

segments.name: The Crossing and the Waiting Years

stops.name: The North Atlantic, the plank driven back
stops.date_confidence: Shaker testimony only, taken down decades later; no log, manifest, or independent witness of the leak or the vision exists
stops.campa: Mid ocean the Mariah springs a plank and takes water faster than the crew can work the pumps. Shaker testimony holds that Ann Lee comes up on deck, tells the captain that the ship will make port because she has seen it make port, and that a wave then strikes the hull and drives the plank back into place. No log, no manifest, and no witness outside the party records any of it. It is the first of the miracles her followers will write down, and the pattern of all of them: the event is known only from the people it converted.
suggested_refs: The Shaker Testimonies account of the leak aboard the Mariah, uncorroborated by any maritime record
sources: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.)

stops.name: New York, the landing at the East River
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia and the National Park Service; Appletons' Cyclopaedia gives May 1774 instead, and the coordinate is the eighteenth-century shoreline rather than the modern landfill
stops.campa: The Mariah comes in at New York on the sixth of August, into a port two years short of a war. Nine English sectarians step ashore with almost nothing, into a town of twenty thousand that has never heard of them and has no reason to. They have no land, no meeting house, no money, and no plan past the vision. Within weeks the party breaks up to find wages wherever wages are, and the woman they call Mother goes into service washing other people's linen.
suggested_refs: The Whitehall Slip and East River wharves of 1774, the working waterfront where the party came ashore
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Queen Street, the Cunningham house
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia names the Cunningham family and Queen Street; the month is inferred from the August landing
stops.campa: She lodges with the Cunningham family on Queen Street, near the East River docks, and works as a laundry assistant. Abraham Stanley finds a forge. For five years this is the whole American history of the Shakers: hired rooms, other people's washing, and a handful of English immigrants scattered across the province after work. Queen Street is now Pearl Street. In those five years nothing is preached in public, nothing is built, and nobody joins. The vision of 1772 has so far produced a laundry.
suggested_refs: Queen Street, lower Manhattan, renamed Pearl Street after the Revolution

stops.name: New York, the years of waiting
stops.date_confidence: the dispersal and the long wait are attested; this coordinate is the atlas's canonical lower Manhattan pin, inherited from the Bellamy file, and not a documented address of Lee's
stops.campa: The waiting runs from the landing to the end of the decade, five years and more with nothing to show. The party is scattered, the money is gone, the war has started, and the vision has produced nothing anyone can point at. She holds the group together by exhortation, repeated so often that the Testimonies record it as a habit rather than a speech. A century later Edward Bellamy will take a desk on Park Row, a few streets from here, and write the republic of common property into a novel that sells half a million copies.
stops.quote: God has not sent us into this land in vain, but He has sent us to bring the gospel to this nation.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. II, v. 12, recorded as a recurring exhortation of the waiting years
suggested_refs: The dispersal of the Mariah party across the New York province, 1774 to 1779
sources: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.)

stops.name: New York, Abraham Stanley leaves
stops.date_confidence: no source gives a year: Wikipedia records the threat and the departure without a date, Appletons' gives no date, and the 1776 and 1777 datings in circulation are unsourced
stops.campa: Abraham Stanley will not live under the celibate rule his wife now preaches. He tells her that if she does not relent he will take up with a prostitute, and he leaves soon after. No source gives a year for it. Thirteen years of marriage, four dead children, and one Atlantic crossing end without a single document, and no account records where he went or what became of him. From here she is Mother Ann and nothing else; the surname Stanley falls out of the story entirely.
suggested_refs: The undated separation of Ann Lee and Abraham Stanley, one of the largest holes in the record
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Niskayuna, Hocknell takes the lease
stops.date_confidence: attested by Wikipedia and the Watervliet Shaker Historic District record; no month is given
stops.campa: John Hocknell leases a tract of wet wooded ground at Niskayuna, in the township of Watervliet, eight miles northwest of Albany, and the scattered party comes together on it at last. They drain, clear, and build. It is swamp that nobody local wants, which is exactly why they can have it. The Believers number perhaps a dozen adults. This is the first Shaker place in America, and every village the movement raises afterwards, from Maine to Kentucky, is laid out against the memory of it.
suggested_refs: The Hocknell lease of 1779 at Niskayuna, first ground held by Shakers in America

stops.name: Niskayuna, the Dark Day
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Dark Day falls on 19 May 1780 and Wikipedia places her public opening of the testimony in that month
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of May the sky over New England goes dark at midday, dark enough that the fowls go to roost and candles are lit at noon. The preachers say judgement; the farmers say smoke off the northern fires. Into that atmosphere Ann Lee opens her testimony publicly for the first time since the landing, six years after coming ashore with nothing. The seekers who have spent the spring waiting for the end of the world begin walking up to Niskayuna to find her.
stops.quote: I can see great numbers coming now, and you will soon see them coming in great numbers.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. II, v. 14, to her brother William Lee
suggested_refs: New England's Dark Day, 19 May 1780, and the wave of seekers it produced

stops.name: New Lebanon, the revival empties toward Niskayuna
stops.date_confidence: Appletons' places the New Lebanon revival at the beginning of 1780; the claim that a Shaker society was gathered there that year is false, the society dates from 1787, and Joseph Meacham's presence in 1780 is tradition rather than documented
stops.campa: A New Light revival breaks out at New Lebanon over the hills to the southeast and burns itself out without producing the second coming its converts had been promised. Word of the Englishwoman in the Niskayuna swamp reaches them inside their disappointment. They come in parties, argue for hours, stay days, and go home Shakers. No society exists at New Lebanon yet; the hill will not be gathered until 1787, three years after she is dead, under Joseph Meacham.
stops.quote: Can you now go home to Lebanon and testify that you have found a woman that told you all things?
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. IV, v. 19, to John Farrington
suggested_refs: The New Light revival at New Lebanon, whose disappointed converts became the first American Shakers
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Albany, arrested for treason
stops.date_confidence: contested: Appletons' dates the Albany treason arrest to summer 1776, which conflicts with the party still being in New York City until 1779; standard Shaker accounts give July 1780, unverified from a reachable source; Wikipedia's article records only the refusal of the oath and no arrest at all
stops.campa: She is taken up as an enemy of the state: an Englishwoman, in the fourth year of the war, whose people will not swear the oath of allegiance and will not carry a musket for either side. The charge is treason, the accusation is that she is talking men out of the militia, and the jail is at Albany. Neutrality is unintelligible in 1780 to both armies. The Shakers will refuse every war fought on this continent for the next two centuries, and will pay for each refusal in the same coin.
suggested_refs: The Albany colonial jail of 1780, building unidentified in the sources
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Poughkeepsie, the jail and the governor's release
stops.date_confidence: contested: Appletons' gives 1777 and a pardon by Governor George Clinton, who took office only in July 1777, leaving no room for the sequence it describes; the standard dating is a transfer from Albany and release in December 1780, which could not be independently verified this session
stops.campa: She is moved down the Hudson to the jail at Poughkeepsie and held there, out of reach of her people, while petitions circulate on both sides. Governor George Clinton orders her released. No evidence of treason is ever produced, and the cost of holding her has begun to exceed the cost of letting her go. She comes back up the river to Niskayuna with the imprisonment converted into an advertisement, and the persecuted Englishwoman is now a name from Albany to the Connecticut line.
suggested_refs: George Clinton's order of release, cited by Appletons' Cyclopaedia with an impossible date
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Niskayuna, setting out east
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia dates the departure to spring 1781 and the tour to roughly two years
stops.campa: In the spring she sets out from Niskayuna with a small company: her brother William, James Whittaker, and a handful of others, on foot and on horseback, into Massachusetts and Connecticut. The tour will run two years and four months. They carry no money and lodge with whoever will take them. She is forty five, has never travelled in this country, and is walking into towns that have already been told she is a British spy, a witch, and a man in women's clothes.
stops.quote: God has called you to take up your cross, and obey the gospel.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. IV, v. 8, to David Meacham of Enfield, Connecticut, January 1781
suggested_refs: The two-year New England preaching tour, 1781 to 1783, the only sustained travel of her American years

stops.name: Mount Washington, the Osborn house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the coordinate matches the listed Benjamin Osborn House, but Wikipedia says only that the party often stayed in homes and never names the Osborns; the identification comes from Shaker local history
stops.campa: The party crosses the New York line into the Taconic hills and lodges at the Osborn house at Mount Washington, first of the friendly roofs that make the whole mission possible. The pattern is set here and repeated for two years: a sympathetic family, a room cleared of its furniture, neighbours filling the doorway, and worship going on past midnight until the frame of the house shakes. Shaker local history keeps the Osborn name. The general accounts of the mission keep only the practice.
stops.quote: I have seen you before, in vision. You must go forth and preach the gospel.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. IV, v. 20, to Ebenezer Cooley
suggested_refs: The Benjamin Osborn House, Mount Washington, Massachusetts, listed on the National Register
sources: Shaker local histories of the Berkshire towns

stops.name: Harvard, the Square House
stops.date_confidence: attested that she took the Square House and that Harvard became the first Massachusetts settlement; the month of arrival is not recorded
stops.campa: At Harvard she finds a house and a congregation already waiting for a messiah. Shadrack Ireland had told his followers he would not die, and when he died they kept the body unburied in the cellar in expectation of his return. Ann Lee takes the Square House and the people inside it. It becomes the first Shaker settlement in Massachusetts and the base of the eastern mission for the better part of two years, and the town of Harvard spends those two years trying to drive her out of it.
stops.quote: I would not give way to unbelief; it is a damning sin.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. VI, v. 16, to Abel Allen, who first saw her at Harvard
suggested_refs: The Square House at Harvard, Massachusetts, inherited from Shadrack Ireland's millennialists
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Shirley, dragged from the house
stops.date_confidence: the mob violence of the mission is attested in general terms by Wikipedia, which lists no towns; the Shirley episode and its date come from Shaker local history
stops.campa: At Shirley the crowd does not stop to argue. She is dragged out of the house where she lodges, struck, threatened, and the party is driven from the town. She walks back into Shirley afterwards, on foot, and holds a meeting in the town that beat her. The episode and its date come down through local Shaker history and appear in no general account of the mission. A Shaker society will be gathered at Shirley within a decade of her death and will keep its meeting house for a hundred and sixty years.
stops.quote: Kneel down, you haughty creature, and confess your sins.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. V, to Hannah Knapp
suggested_refs: The Shirley Shaker village site, gathered after her death on ground where she was assaulted
sources: Shaker local histories of Middlesex County

stops.name: Petersham, the house surrounded
stops.date_confidence: tradition: nineteenth-century Shaker histories name Petersham, the general accounts of the mission describe the violence without listing towns
stops.campa: Tradition places one of the worst attacks at Petersham, in the high country west of Worcester. The shape of it is fixed by now: a magistrate who will not act, a crowd that has been told she is a British agent, a house surrounded after dark, and the Believers carrying her out through the middle of it. She goes on preaching in the same district afterwards. The general histories of the mission record the beatings without naming the towns; Petersham comes down through local Shaker memory alone.
stops.quote: You must begin at the top twigs, and crop them off.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. VI, v. 6, to Hannah Shapley, on overcoming sin by degrees
suggested_refs: Nineteenth-century Shaker histories of the Petersham assault

stops.name: Ashfield, the hill farms
stops.date_confidence: tradition: Ashfield is named in Shaker local history and not confirmed in the sources that attest the mission
stops.campa: In the hill towns above the Connecticut valley she gathers families whose descendants will fill the Shaker villages of western Massachusetts. What she preaches is plain and short: confess what you have done, stop doing it, work with your hands, and hold nothing as your own. The farmers hearing it are in the last years of a war that has taken their sons and ruined the currency, and most of them have nothing left to hold. Ashfield is remembered by the Shakers and not by the general accounts of the tour.
stops.quote: Put down that whip, and hear the word of God, you idle old man!
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. IV, to Hezekiah Hammond
suggested_refs: The Connecticut valley hill farms that supplied the western Massachusetts Shaker villages

stops.name: Enfield, Joseph Meacham comes over
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: her personal visit to Enfield is Shaker tradition, but Joseph Meacham's New Light ministry at Enfield and his later leadership from 1787 are attested; the coordinate is the town centre, not the Shaker Pines site three kilometres east where the village later stood
stops.campa: Across the Connecticut line at Enfield she meets Joseph Meacham, the New Light Baptist minister who has already brought himself and much of his following out of the revival and into her hands. He is the ablest man she will ever convert. After her death he turns a wandering preaching movement into a system of ordered villages with a joint treasury, a written covenant, and men and women governing in pairs. The Shaker village at Enfield is founded in 1793, nine years after she is dead, on ground she is remembered to have walked.
stops.quote: The order of man in the natural creation is a figure of the order of God.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.), Ch. IV, to Joseph Meacham
suggested_refs: Enfield, Connecticut, Joseph Meacham's New Light parish and later a Shaker village

stops.name: New Marlborough, the last winter of the tour
stops.date_confidence: tradition: New Marlborough is named in nineteenth-century Shaker histories and not in the general summary of the mission
stops.campa: The party comes back west through the Berkshire towns in the last winter of the mission, and at New Marlborough a hostile crowd gathers on them again. Two years of this have worn the company down to the bone. Her brother William, the strongest of them and the one who carries her out of the crowds, is taking injuries in these encounters that do not heal. The towns doing the beating will furnish the Hancock and Tyringham societies within five years of her death.
suggested_refs: The Berkshire towns of the return leg, later the ground of the Hancock and Tyringham societies

stops.name: Richmond, the kitchen tables
stops.date_confidence: tradition: Richmond is named in Shaker local history and is not independently confirmed in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Richmond, under the western slope of the Berkshires, holds small clusters of converts made on the outward leg and visited again on the way home. The mission ends the way it began, at kitchen tables, with a woman who cannot read reciting scripture back at ministers who can. Her health is going. The Believers around her have stopped expecting her to see out the decade, and she has begun telling them what they are to do when she is gone, which is chiefly to gather into villages and hold everything in common.
suggested_refs: The scattered Berkshire convert households of 1783

segments.name: The Return and the Two Graves

stops.name: New Lebanon, the converts holding
stops.date_confidence: inferred from the geography of the attested mission; the 1783 itinerary is documented nowhere
stops.campa: She turns north through New Lebanon, where the first American converts came from, and finds them holding. Nothing in the record fixes the route home. The geography fixes it well enough, because there is one road through these hills and these are the people living along it. In four years New Lebanon will be gathered into the central ministry of the whole movement and will govern every Shaker village in America from a hill she is only passing over on her way back to the swamp.
suggested_refs: The hill at New Lebanon, later Mount Lebanon, seat of the Shaker central ministry from 1787

stops.name: Niskayuna, the company comes home broken
stops.date_confidence: attested that she and William Lee returned injured near the end of the mission; the month is inferred from the tour's stated length of two years and four months
stops.campa: She comes back into Niskayuna in the autumn, two years and four months after setting out, injured, worn through, and at the head of a movement that now has believers in three states. What she brings home is a working method: confession, celibacy, common property, and labour as the form that prayer takes. The villages built on that method will make chairs, flat brooms, seed packets, and medicines that the world buys for a century without believing one word of the doctrine behind them.
stops.quote: Put your hands to work and your heart to God, and keep your family to work, and you will be able to pay your debts.
stops.quote_source: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.; compiled by Rufus Bishop, first published 1816)
suggested_refs: Shaker industry: the flat broom, the seed packet, the ladderback chair, all descended from this instruction
sources: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.)

stops.name: Watervliet, the death of William Lee
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 July 1784 by Wikipedia; the attribution of his death to mission injuries is the Shaker account
stops.campa: William Lee, her brother, dies in July of injuries taken on the mission that never healed. He had been the strength of the company through both years of it, the one who carried her out of the crowds at Shirley and Petersham and stood between her and the men who came at night. She does not recover from his death. In the weeks that follow she tells the Believers plainly that she is going after him, and Niskayuna begins preparing for a movement without the woman who is its entire doctrine.
suggested_refs: The grave of William Lee at the Watervliet Shaker cemetery, beside his sister's

stops.name: Watervliet, the death of Mother Ann
stops.date_confidence: attested to 8 September 1784 by Wikipedia, Appletons' and the National Park Service
stops.campa: She dies at Watervliet on the eighth of September, forty eight years old, seven weeks after her brother. The Believers report that she sings in unknown tongues from her rocking chair at the end. She leaves no writing, having never been taught to write, and names no successor in any document. That same year in Paris a royal commission is sitting on Franz Anton Mesmer, examining patients who convulse, cry out, and lose control of their eyes, and finding no magnetic fluid in any of them. The century has two vocabularies for a shaking body and no agreement between them.
suggested_refs: The Shaker testimony of her deathbed singing in unknown tongues, reported and never corroborated
sources: Appletons' Cyclopaedia of American Biography, 'Lee, Ann'

stops.name: Watervliet Shaker cemetery, the burial
stops.date_confidence: the burial beside her brother in the Watervliet Shaker ground is attested; no source consulted gives the day, and the stone has been photographed but never transcribed
stops.campa: She is buried in the Shaker ground at Watervliet beside her brother, under a stone no larger than any other, in a plot where no grave is permitted to outrank its neighbours. The movement at this moment has a few hundred members. Within sixty years it will have six thousand, in eighteen villages from Maine to Kentucky, every one of them celibate, every one holding its property in common, and every one dating itself from a woman in this ground who could not sign her own name.
suggested_refs: The Watervliet Shaker cemetery, Colonie, New York, photographed in 2006 with the inscription never transcribed

stops.name: New Lebanon, the doctrine written down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book and the year; the place of first printing is not established by any source consulted, and this coordinate is the ministry seat rather than a documented press
stops.campa: Benjamin Seth Youngs, with Lucy Wright behind him, publishes The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing, the first systematic statement of what the Shakers believe. Twenty four years after her death the vision in the Manchester cell has become a theology with chapters: four dispensations, a Godhead male and female, and Ann Lee as the second appearing. She had said none of this in these words. What she said was that lust is the fall and confession is the door, and she said it to people who could write it down only from memory.
suggested_refs: The Testimony of Christ's Second Appearing, 1808, the Shaker Bible

stops.name: Watervliet, the Testimonies collected
stops.date_confidence: attested: first published 1816, compiled by Rufus Bishop, revised by Seth Y. Wells, the accessible text being the 1888 edition
stops.campa: The society goes round the surviving witnesses, the men and women who were in the rooms, and prints what they remember her saying. It is the only record of her voice: taken down thirty years late, from people who loved her, and it contains the whip and the top twigs and the birthday and the great numbers coming. Every quotation of Ann Lee in existence comes out of this one book. Nothing she said was written down while she was alive to correct it, because none of the first Believers thought to, and she could not do it herself.
suggested_refs: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Our Ever Blessed Mother Ann Lee, 1816
sources: Testimonies of the Life, Character, Revelations and Doctrines of Mother Ann Lee (Bishop/Wells, 1888 ed.)

stops.name: Watervliet, the Era of Manifestations
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia dates the Era of Manifestations from 1837 into the mid-1850s, not the ten years given in some summaries
stops.campa: Fifty three years after her death the young women of Watervliet begin to shake again. They fall into trance, speak in tongues, draw maps of heaven, and deliver instructions they say come directly from Mother Ann. The Shakers call it Mother Ann's Work. It runs from 1837 into the middle of the following decade, longer than her own ministry lasted. The elders governing by then are men who never saw her, receiving her orders through girls who were not born when she died, and writing the messages into the village records as received.
suggested_refs: The Era of Manifestations, 1837 to the mid-1850s, and the spirit messages entered in the village journals

stops.name: New York, the gift drawings at the Folk Art Museum
stops.date_confidence: the drawings belong to the Era of Manifestations, 1837 to the mid-1850s, and no single year applies; the museum holding is present-day
stops.campa: Out of the manifestations come the gift drawings: watercolours of treasure chests, golden chariots, tables laid in heavenly mansions, made by Hannah Cohoon, Rebecca Landon, Polly Collins, Sarah Bates, Polly Anne Reed and Joseph Wicker, who had never been taught to draw and mostly never drew again. They are unsigned, and the people who made them called them gifts rather than pictures. They hang now in the American Folk Art Museum at Lincoln Square, among the very few objects in New York City that a Shaker of 1845 would recognize.
suggested_refs: The Shaker gift drawings in the American Folk Art Museum collection, 2 Lincoln Square, New York

stops.name: Colonie, the airport on the herb garden
stops.date_confidence: the construction of Albany International Airport on the Shaker community's herb garden is attested; the construction year given here is a placeholder, and whether the work approached the graves is documented nowhere
stops.campa: Albany International Airport is built on the Watervliet Shakers' herb garden, the ground that grew the physic the society dried, packeted, and sold across the country. The cemetery lies just past the field. No source consulted says how close the construction came to the graves. Aircraft climb out over the plot where the founder of American celibate communism is buried, on the site of the first Shaker settlement in the world, and a historic district sign is the only thing on the ground that says so.
suggested_refs: Albany International Airport, built over the Watervliet Shaker herb garden

stops.name: Sabbathday Lake, the last three
stops.date_confidence: attested as of 2025
stops.campa: At Sabbathday Lake in New Gloucester, Maine, three Shakers remain: June Carpenter, Arnold Hadd, and April Baxter, who joined in 2025. They keep thirteen thousand artifacts, a research library, and the observance of Mother Ann's Day on the first Sunday in August, which commemorates the landing of 1774. It is the last active Shaker community on earth. An order that requires celibacy of everyone who enters it has been recruiting, one adult convert at a time, for two hundred and fifty years.
suggested_refs: Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village, New Gloucester, Maine, and its observance of Mother Ann's Day

stops.name: Venice, the testament filmed
stops.date_confidence: attested: the premiere is dated 1 September 2025 at the Venice International Film Festival
stops.campa: The Testament of Ann Lee premieres at the Venice film festival, Mona Fastvold directing, Amanda Seyfried as Mother Ann, the worship staged as musical numbers. John Fowles had already appended her to A Maggot in 1985; Reg Meuross had already sung The Heart of Ann Lee in 2010. An illiterate Manchester mill girl who forbade her followers to reproduce is carried forward by everything except descendants. Two hundred and forty one years after her death an audience on the Lido watches a room full of people shake.
suggested_refs: The Testament of Ann Lee, dir. Mona Fastvold, Venice International Film Festival, 1 September 2025
